children: Bitcoin has a quantum problem, and better math alone won't fix it. The harder part is logistics.

Glassnode's May 2026 estimate put the amount of exposed BTC at approximately 6.04 million coins. Broader research estimates put the figure at 6 to 7 million BTC, or roughly 30 to 35% of total supply. Those coins sit in addresses whose public keys are already visible on the blockchain.

That matters because public keys are what a future quantum computer would need to attack. Bitcoin's developers have proposals on the table to protect those coins. Fixing the cryptography is only half the job. They also have to get millions of coins, plus the exchanges, custodians and bridges that hold them, onto the new system.

Bitcoin secures ownership with elliptic-curve cryptography, specifically a curve called secp256k1. Think of it as a lock that is trivial to close but practically impossible to pick with today's computers.

A sufficiently powerful quantum machine running Shor's algorithm changes that equation. In theory, it could work backward from a visible public key to the private key that controls the funds. Once that happens, the coins belong to whoever did the math first.

Not every Bitcoin address is equally vulnerable. The weakest are older addresses using the legacy P2PK format, where the public key sits openly on the chain. Approximately 1.7 million BTC are held in these structurally vulnerable addresses.

Address reuse adds to the pile. When a holder sends and receives through the same address repeatedly, their public key can end up exposed. That habit pushes the total well beyond the P2PK coins alone.
For now, the danger is theoretical. No practical quantum computer capable of breaking Bitcoin's signatures exists today.

The technical proposals exist, at least on paper. BIP-360 and BIP-361 aim to introduce new signature schemes and a phased move away from legacy signatures. As of November 2026, both remain in draft status, and neither has an activation timeline.
The real fight is philosophical. One camp wants to restrict coins that never migrate to quantum-resistant addresses. The other wants upgrades to stay voluntary. Neither approach has been adopted.

Each option comes with an uncomfortable trade-off. Restricting unmigrated coins could protect the network from a sudden flood of stolen BTC. It would also mean the protocol effectively decides what happens to coins whose owners never moved them, a sore point for a system built on the idea that nobody can touch your funds.

Voluntary upgrades avoid that problem but create another. Coins that stay put stay exposed. If those keys are ever cracked, attackers could walk off with a meaningful slice of supply. Early adopters who left holdings dormant sit at the center of this concern, since their coins are disproportionately likely to live in old address formats.

There has been movement on the engineering side. StarkWare carried out what it described as the first quantum-safe Bitcoin transaction on mainnet in August 2026. Blockstream has been testing post-quantum signatures.

Regulators are watching too. IOSCO's November 2026 report highlighted the complexities tied to upgrading Bitcoin's cryptography. Regulatory reports more broadly have flagged the challenges of larger signature sizes and the potential for network congestion during a transition.

Those last two points deserve attention. Post-quantum signatures tend to be bulkier than the ones Bitcoin uses today. Bigger signatures take up more block space, and a mass migration of millions of coins could crowd the network at the same time.
Meanwhile, some other blockchains have already started rolling out quantum-resistant security. Bitcoin, the largest and most conservative network in crypto, is still debating the approach.

The infrastructure layer is where the work gets messy. Exchanges, custodians and bridges collectively manage enormous amounts of BTC on behalf of users. Each of them would need to upgrade wallets, signing systems and internal processes, ideally without disrupting deposits and withdrawals. Custodians serving institutions will likely face questions from clients and regulators about their readiness, especially with IOSCO already highlighting upgrade complexity.

What to watch next: whether BIP-360 or BIP-361 moves beyond draft, whether developers converge on a stance for dormant coins, and whether firms like StarkWare and Blockstream push their testing into broader production use.

title: Bitcoin faces a quantum security challenge with roughly 6 million coins exposed
